description: We're a duo developer team passionate about exploring Earth science through data and technology. We're taking on the Be an Earth System Trend Detective! challenge to analyse NASA's Earth observation datasets, uncover meaningful environmental trends, and turn complex scientific data into clear, interactive visualisations. Our goal is to make Earth system changes easier to understand through technology, data analysis, and creative problem-solving.
summary: Procella is a 3D globe-trotter game that turns NASA's climate record into places you can visit. Pick a traveller, a vehicle, a year from 1981 to 2025 and any spot on Earth. You land in that place's real terrain, under the weather NASA recorded there that month. The people you meet tell you how their climate has changed, quoting that place's own NASA data. A trend dossier then tests each change: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant. Every verdict shows its slope, confidence interval, record length and method, so students learn to read evidence, not just look at it. By Priyanshu Naskar and Daksh Dayalani
details:
What it does: Procella answers the challenge's four questions (what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant) inside a game a student wants to play. A traveller lands anywhere on Earth in any year from 1981 to 2025. Rain, cloud, wind, haze and snow come from NASA POWER for that exact place and month, and each effect can be switched on or off to see which variable drives it. People under gold beacons tell short climate stories built from that location's own 45-year record, and the trend dossier backs every story with the numbers.

How it works: NASA POWER is called live for monthly and annual series of 10 variables: temperature, daytime high, night-time low, rainfall, wind, humidity, root-zone soil wetness, cloud, surface sunlight and aerosol haze. The statistics engine runs a tie-corrected Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope with a 95% confidence interval, refuses to judge records shorter than 15 years, and was verified against the pymannkendall Python package. Every verdict states the slope, its confidence interval, the p-value, the number of years and the method. Verdicts come in three honest states: Detected, Not detectable yet, and Too short to judge. "Not significant" is reported as "no detectable trend", never "no change". A start-year slider re-runs the test from later years so students see how fragile a trend can be, and the record can be played as sound. Globe Lab scans trends across the planet live, compares two variables, and projects forward; the Future Zone extrapolates past 2025 with honest ranges, clearly labelled as a straight-line extrapolation, not a forecast.

The world: real SRTM elevation, 10 m satellite imagery, NASA GIBS imagery on the globe, and vegetation chosen by each place's long-term temperature and rainfall. The sun sits where it really was for that date and hour. 30 world cities are rebuilt from OpenStreetMap buildings, roads, parks and water, with 37 landmarks modelled at real size. Nine vehicles (4x4, saloon, buggy, light aircraft, helicopter, float plane and three boats) have physics tuned to published figures. 18 advancements reward exploring different eras.

Benefits and impact: climate trends usually arrive as a chart on a page. Procella makes them local, visual and testable. A student can stand in a city in 1985 and again in 2025, see the difference, and then check whether that difference is a real trend or noise. We want students to learn to ask "is this trend real?" before believing a claim, and to have a free tool for exploring their own region.

Tools: JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), three.js and EZ-Tree for 3D, the Web Audio API for procedural sound, and Python for data checks and the city data pipeline. Hosted as a static site on Netlify. Open source under the MIT licence.

Use of AI: we used an AI coding assistant to help write and debug code, research and verify data sources, convert our slides to a web page and draft documentation. All statistics were verified against pymannkendall, and all climate data is fetched live from NASA, never generated.

Github Link: https://github.com/itzblaze-10/Procella
dataRefs: NASA POWER API (MERRA-2, CERES SYN1deg, GEWEX SRB, GPM IMERG derived), called live
MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA GMAO), via NASA POWER
CERES SYN1deg (cloud, haze, sunlight), via NASA POWER
GEWEX SRB (sunlight 1984 to 2000), via NASA POWER
GPM IMERG rainfall (POWER daily and GIBS layer)
NASA GIBS imagery services (WMS and WMTS)
MODIS Terra Corrected Reflectance true colour (GIBS)
projectRefs: OpenStreetMap data via Overpass API and Nominatim (ODbL 1.0): city buildings, roads, water, parks, place names
Sentinel-2 cloudless 2020 by EOX IT Services, modified Copernicus Sentinel data (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0): ground imagery
AWS Terrain Tiles (SRTM, GMTED2010, ETOPO1): elevation tiles
EZ-Tree by Daniel Greenheck (MIT): procedural trees and rock models
Poly Haven textures (CC0): ground and building surfaces
pymannkendall (MIT): reference used to verify our statistics
